title: On-call and Incident Response Playbook and Templates
author: Avery Chen
body:
Overview
--------
This playbook documents Redwood Inference's on-call and incident response process. It contains the incident lifecycle, runbook templates, postmortem template, on-call rotation best practices, game day guidance, and customer/status-page communications templates. Intended audience: on-call engineers, SREs, incident commanders, support, and engineering managers.

Scope
-----
Applies to all production-facing services in Redwood's hosted and dedicated deployments, the public API, control plane services, and telemetry/observability pipelines.

Key definitions and severity levels
---------------------------------
1) Sev 1 (P0) – System-wide outage or data-loss affecting >50% of customers or violating critical SLA (example: API responses return 500 for most requests). Requires immediate paging and IC activation.
2) Sev 2 (P1) – Partial outage or severe degradation affecting a subset of customers (>5%) or key features (embeddings, auth). Escalate to on-call SRE and relevant service owners.
3) Sev 3 (P2) – Functional degradation with mitigation, increased error rates, or noncritical performance regression. Track and triage in triage channel.
4) Sev 4 (P3) – Informational/maintenance events, planned degradations, or low-impact bugs.

Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------
- Pager / Primary Responder: First to acknowledge, attempt containment, triage, and execute safe mitigations.
- Incident Commander (IC): Coordinates the response, assigns tasks, and runs the incident timeline. Usually the most senior on-call or designated IC.
- Communications Lead: Owns customer and internal comms, updates the status page and slack channels.
- Subject Matter Experts (SMEs): Service owners and engineers called in for deep debugging.
- Postmortem Author: Owns the end-to-end postmortem write-up and follow-ups.

Incident response process (step-by-step)
---------------------------------------
1) Detection & Alerting
   - Alerts originate from monitoring (metrics, logs, tracing) or customer reports. The alert should include: service, symptom, trigger, links to runbooks and dashboards.
2) Acknowledge (within 5 minutes for Sev 1/2)
   - Pager acknowledges on-call and updates Slack channel #incidents-prod.
3) Triage (first 10 minutes)
   - Determine severity, affected services/customers, scope, and immediate impact.
   - IC selected if severity >= Sev 2.
4) Containment (0–30 minutes)
   - Apply safe mitigations (traffic shift, revert rollout, scale up, enable fallback model variant). Document commands run and reasons.
5) Communication (ongoing)
   - Publish initial status page entry and internal summary. Provide cadence for updates (every 15 minutes for Sev 1, 30–60 minutes for Sev 2).
6) Remediation and Root Cause Analysis (RCA)
   - After containment, work on permanent fix. Collect logs, traces, heap dumps, and config diffs.
7) Recovery & Verification
   - Confirm with synthetic checks and customer verification where appropriate.
8) Post-incident review and postmortem (within 72 hours)
   - Produce postmortem, assign action items, and schedule follow-ups.

Runbook template (quick reference)
----------------------------------
Title: <service> - <symptom> runbook
Owner: <team>
Pager: <pager-on-call-role/contact>
Severity: <Sev 1/2/3>
Detection: <metric/alert rule link>
Dashboard: <link to dashboard>
Play (ordered steps):
  1) Acknowledge alert and post to #incidents-prod.
  2) Check recent deploys: `git log`, `k8s rollout status`.
  3) Run quick health checks: `curl -I https://<service>/health` and `curl -s https://<service>/metrics | grep errors`.
  4) If error spike is seen, attempt safe rollback or scale: `kubectl rollout undo`, `kubectl scale deployment <svc> --replicas=<n>`.
  5) If latencies high, enable fallback routing: route to model-variant-low-latency (see routing-runbook).
Escalation path: 
  - 10 minutes -> notify service owner 
  - 20 minutes -> escalate to eng-sre lead 
  - 30 minutes -> IC declared
Post-incident checklist: incident ticket created, status page updated, postmortem assigned.

Postmortem template (required fields)
-------------------------------------
- Title
- Authors (list)
- Incident date/time (start and end)
- Severity
- Summary (short, <3 sentences)
- Timeline (ordered timestamps and actions)
- Root cause (concise)
- Contributing factors
- Corrective and preventive actions (with owners and ETA)
- Customer impact (who and how long)
- Detection & response metrics (MTTD, MTTR, time to acknowledge, number of pages)
- Follow-ups and verification plan

Escalation and paging policy
----------------------------
- Pager rotation managed in PagerDuty (or configured tool). On-call engineer must acknowledge within 5 minutes for Sev1/2.
- If no acknowledgement after 5 minutes, escalate to secondary and team lead. After 15 minutes escalate to engineering manager and SRE director.

SLOs & alert thresholds (examples)
----------------------------------
| SLO / Alert | Threshold | Severity |
|-------------|-----------|----------|
| API 99th latency | > 2s sustained for 5m | Sev2 |
| 5xx rate | > 1% of traffic for 5m | Sev1 |
| Downstream error rate (DB) | > 5% | Sev1 |
| Token generation error | any data-loss or corruption | Sev1 |

On-call rotation & best practices
---------------------------------
- Rotation length: 1 week preferred (min 5 days). For small teams consider 2-week rotation with staggered backups.
- Handover note: outgoing on-call must write a 10–15 minute handover summarizing ongoing incidents, scheduled maintenance, and flaky alerts.
- Quiet hours: limit non-urgent paging during local nights where possible; use escalation for critical events.
- Compensation & training: ensure on-call pay and regular training for new on-call engineers.

Game days (regular practice)
---------------------------
Purpose: Validate runbooks, exercise escalation paths, and test tooling under controlled failure.
Frequency: Quarterly per critical service; at least annually for noncritical services.
Typical plan:
  1) Pre-game checklist: scope, participants, game-day owner, no-customer-impact constraint.
  2) Inject failure (e.g., remove a replica, increase latency with tc/netem, introduce a faulty config).
  3) Observe detection, paging, triage, containment, and recovery.
  4) Debrief and update runbooks and on-call docs.

Status page and customer communications templates
------------------------------------------------
Use clear, consistent language. Keep templated fields: incident id, affected product, start time, current status, impact, mitigation, next update ETA, and contact link.

Initial acknowledgment (public):
- Title: Incident {INC-<id>}: {service} degraded
- Body: We are aware of increased errors affecting {service}. Start time: {YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC}. Impact: {brief impact summary}. Current status: Investigating. Next update: in 15 minutes.

Customer update (example):
- Title: Incident {INC-<id>}: mitigation in progress
- Body: We have identified a change in {subsystem}. Mitigation: routing to fallback cluster and rolling back recent deploy. Impact reduced to {X%} of customers. ETA for full recovery: ~45 minutes.

Resolved notice (public):
- Title: Incident {INC-<id>}: resolved
- Body: The issue impacting {service} has been resolved at {YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC}. Root cause: {brief root cause}. Actions taken: {list of immediate fixes and planned follow-ups}. Postmortem will be published within 72 hours.

Internal Slack templates
------------------------
Initial incident message (channel #incidents-prod):
  :rotating_light: Sev {n} - {service} - {short symptom}
  Pager: @<pager>
  IC: TBD
  Link: <incident-ticket> | <dashboard>
  First actions: acknowledge, triage, contain.

Postmortem publishing checklist
-------------------------------
- Postmortem drafted and reviewed by SMEs.
- Action items assigned with owners and ETAs.
- Postmortem published to Confluence and linked from incident ticket.
- Follow-up verification scheduled and completed.

Measurement and continuous improvement
-------------------------------------
We track MTTD (mean time to detect), MTTA (acknowledgement), MTTR (time to resolve), and number of repeated incidents per service. Game day results and postmortem actions feed into reliability initiatives and SLO tuning.

Where to find more resources
---------------------------
- SLO & error budget docs: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets
- Runbook authoring guide: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks
- Incident ticket template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-ticket-template

Ownership and maintenance
-------------------------
This document is owned by Eng-SRE and maintained quarterly. Update the runbooks after any incident or game day.

Appendix: Useful commands and links
----------------------------------
- k8s: `kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=<svc>`; `kubectl logs -f <pod>`
- Observability: dashboards links (traces, perf, errors) – add service-specific dashboards to runbook.
- Pager workflow: PagerDuty escalation policy: PD-Product-Prod-Oncall

Contact
-------
For questions about the runbook or process, contact the Eng-SRE team: eng-sre@redwood-inference.com
